body:
Let’s say you have some inside information about a matter of interest.  What is the best way to line your pockets by making money on prediction markets?  
You don’t. 
This is going to be quite disappointing to some ethically questionable individuals working in Hollywood, or business, or allegedly even our military, but it’s true.
When it comes to insider trading, there is no sweet spot. 
Let me begin by describing some of the goals of this little project that you have so graciously decided to join on the ground level. There are a bunch of stretch hopes like building an audience the size of Joe Rogan’s multiplied by late-90’s Rush Limbaugh audience.  There’s a fleet of Bugattis that I want us all to be able to purchase with our profits. There’s also trying to make our diet of election and political coverage suck about 0.1% less.
But perhaps my first goal is to help the vast majority of the media reach a first-grade level of comprehension of prediction markets while writing about prediction markets.  To be clear, this does not mean that every journalist can be described as medically brain-dead on this topic.  While in Washington DC this week, I probably met with two dozen journalists and media members, many of whom asked very interesting and thoughtful questions.  
For the others, I beg of you. 
Know something about the something you’re talking about. 
Allow me to provide a typical example, which comes to us from a relatively smart newsletter. 
In the prediction market era, almost anyone can bet on anything—from the Nicolás Maduro’s ouster to the ‘Outer Banks’ release date—even if they have privileged knowledge that makes betting a sure thing.
The only problem with this sentence is that it is completely false in every measurable way.  The actions described here are a crime.  Not morally questionable or ethically iffy…a literal crime.  
If you want to be super duper kind, I suppose you could argue that you “can” do almost anything.  In the same way, one could write “in this era of automobiles, almost anyone can run over a bus stop filled with kindergartners.”  Yeah, I suppose you “can” do this.  But, we have associated criminal penalties tied to these actions, which leaves all that murder a little less appetizing for most people. 
In case you don’t believe me, I directly asked the person responsible for overseeing prediction markets, CFTC Chair Michael Selig. 
I could give you a thousand different examples of media members not understanding this (or, as in the case of this newsletter, heavily downplaying the context), but I’ll limit myself to one more:
I know a guy who does work for a CBS competition show (you can guess which
one), and he’s been making a little side money on the prediction apps. It’s
actually pretty easy.
Yes, people do break the law.  Sometimes, it probably is easy. What is certain is that every time there is a suspicion of lawbreaking related to prediction markets, the media is there to tell us all about it..  And, I am 
oh so very sure 
they are 
incredibly concerned
 over all of this fraud and manipulation.  A guy might have made thousands 
pointing a hairdryer at a thermometer in France
! The media is on the case!
Oddly, very few of these same sources cared at all when 
Minnesota taxpayers were being bilked out of $9 billion
.  Or the nearly 
unlimited funds stolen from various COVID programs
. Or the 
twelve figure sum currently being wasted on train to nowhere 
 being overseen by the guy who is arguably leading the pack for the democratic presidential nomination. Or how 
Nancy Pelosi just happens to be the greatest investor in the history of the universe
.
“A little side money”
The key phrase in the piece is “a little side money.” 
Is it theoretically possible to make “a little side money” off of some insider information?  For the moment, let’s grant this point. 
If you work on Survivor and know the outcome of Survivor, you could put some money into a market about Survivor and make a little side money off of Survivor.
But, at what cost?
You’re going to prison
You might not think it’s a big deal because it’s only about a television show, or it’s only a few bucks, or whatever other justification you’ve conjured.  But, my advice would be to think about where the lines are and stay far away from them.  
Yes, prediction markets are fun. But they are real financial markets.  They are really regulated by the government. People really go to jail for insider trading. You’re risking this to make “a little side money?”
As these stories continue to surface, the government and these companies are going to look for people to make examples out of.  Don’t be one of them. 
The reality of the media adoring these stories so much, combined with the fact that you are stupid enough to tell one of the most connected Hollywood reporters in America that you are engaging in illegal behavior surrounding a major studio, should be enough of self-evident warning to stop what you are doing immediately.
You’re going to lose your job 
Even if you avoid legal consequences, if you get caught doing this you are surely going to lose your job. You’re essentially leaking details about who won your stupid reality show into a public forum, and if you get snagged, you will be fired. The fakey drama is the product. You’re risking ruining the work of hundreds of people and millions of dollars in production costs, so that you can make “a little extra money.” Is this worth the risk of your six or seven-figure income? Even your five-figure income?
The prediction markets are not the bad guys in this scenario: you are. 
It’s just a few bucks, they’ll never know
You might be right.  It might work. You might make a few hundred bucks without anyone noticing. But, you also might get 
publicly humiliated and fined for throwing $50 on your own campaign
. They can and do catch these things, even when it’s just a few bucks.
US-based exchanges have Know Your Customer rules that they must follow. They know who you are.  If they get a whiff of this stuff, it will be easy to figure out who you are and how you are connected to the information that has supplied your amazing clairvoyance.  And these companies are incentivized to make an example out of you. They don’t have to announce these enforcement actions, but they usually do.
Why? These are companies that are worth tens of billions of dollars. They are trying to avoid looking irresponsible in order to dodge legislation that will limit their growth by tens of billions of additional dollars. As enticing as it is for them to look the other way to get ahold of the eight bucks they make off your transaction, I wouldn’t count on this keeping you out of trouble. 
But people are making hundreds of thousands of dollars off this!
The media has been highlighting stories like this whenever they can dig them up.  Most infamously, this week, a soldier was charged with making around $400,000 because of his prior knowledge of the Maduro operation.  
To be absolutely clear, if true, this is absolutely horrible. It could have put American lives at risk. It could have caused the operation to end in catastrophe. It should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. 
However, here are some facts of which you should be aware:
It is being prosecuted 
to the fullest extent of the law
. People commit crimes all the time.  We have a legal system to deal with them.  That’s what is happening.
The Venezuela story, along with almost every other one you have heard about this side of 
Mr. Beast employees
, has happened on overseas exchanges.  No amount of legislation suggested by Elizabeth Warren is going to change their availability.  In fact, the dumber our legislation becomes here in the US, the more of this activity will be driven to overseas markets.
There is no sweet spot.
The problem with your secret illegal retirement plan is simple.
If you go small, and try to make “a little extra money”, it is possible that you’ll get away with it. Just like it’s possible that you’ll get away with grabbing a pack of Devil Dogs on every third visit to Circle K. But, if you’re going small, the risk of your job, a fine, or a visit from authorities isn’t worth it. Do a little cost-benefit analysis, will ya?
If you go big, you might even get the rush of turning a few thousand bucks into hundreds of thousands. That’s worth risking your job and future as a law-abiding  citizen, right?  
Here’s the thing: If you are on a US-based exchange, and you throw a bunch of cash into an impossible long shot which magically hits two days later, THEY ARE GOING TO NOTICE.
Every one of these places is dumping millions of dollars into detection systems that utilize advanced AI, along with good old-fashioned annoying human beings. And, they already know who you are, along with a lot of information about you, which you had to confirm with them as a legal condition of opening the account. 
So, why not go overseas?  Well, you can probably do that if you really want to. But, those exchanges are typically operating through a blockchain system. What does this mean? It means every time you throw money down, it is public. They might not know your name, but they can see what you have done. There’s an entire cottage industry of obsessives flagging suspicious transactions on the daily. Once they are aware of what has happened, authorities can almost always figure out who you are, unless you’re already highly skilled in criminal activity.
So, how do you properly conduct your insider trading?
If you’re asking yourself “would this be insider trading?” it’s probably too close to the line and not worth the risk, even if you’re actually in the clear. Plus, you never know when some annoying government employee or irritating co-worker is going to decide to make your life miserable. 
You might think you’re smart enough to pull this off.  And maybe you are?  But, I refer you to the immortal words of Michael Bolton—the Office Space guy, not the singer:
You know what I can’t figure out? How is it that all these stupid Neanderthal Mafia guys can be so good at crime, and smart guys like us can suck so badly at it?
So, in conclusion, let’s say you have some inside information about a matter of interest.  What is the best way to line your pockets making money on prediction markets?  
You don’t.
